proof:
Source: steps 0, 2 and 3 of the parent proof (the hypothesis (H) applied to the dilates g(t⁻¹·)).
Hypotheses: μ is a measure on ℝ^N = Euclidean N (Borel σ-algebra) with μ(K) < ∞ for every compact K (IsFiniteMeasureOnCompacts μ), n ∈ ℕ, and
 (H) ∫ (n·h(y) + Dh(y)(y)) dμ(y) = 0 for every C¹ function h : ℝ^N → ℝ with compact support, where Dh(y) := fderiv ℝ h y.
Fix a C¹ function g : ℝ^N → ℝ with compact support and t > 0; write c := t⁻¹ (so c ≠ 0) and Dg := fderiv ℝ g. We prove n·∫ g(c·y) dμ(y) + ∫ Dg(c·y)(c·y) dμ(y) = 0.
1. (Integrability principle.) Every continuous f : ℝ^N → ℝ with compact support is μ-integrable: it is bounded and vanishes outside the compact set tsupport f, which has finite μ-measure (Continuous.integrable_of_hasCompactSupport, using IsFiniteMeasureOnCompacts μ).
2. (The dilate is C¹ with compact support.) Let g_c(y) := g(c·y). The map y ↦ c·y is a continuous linear map, hence C^∞ (contDiff_id.const_smul c), so g_c = g ∘ (y ↦ c·y) is C¹ (ContDiff.comp). Its support is c⁻¹·(support g); since y ↦ c·y is a homeomorphism of ℝ^N (c ≠ 0), tsupport g_c is the image of the compact set tsupport g under y ↦ c⁻¹·y, hence compact (HasCompactSupport.comp_smul with c ≠ 0).
3. (Derivative of the dilate.) g is C¹, hence differentiable at every point (ContDiff.differentiable, as 1 ≠ 0). The map y ↦ c·y has derivative c·id at every y (hasFDerivAt_id together with HasFDerivAt.const_smul). By the chain rule (HasFDerivAt.comp), Dg_c(y) = Dg(c·y) ∘ (c·id), so for every y, Dg_c(y)(y) = Dg(c·y)(c·y).
4. (The two summands are integrable.) (a) y ↦ n·g(c·y) is a constant multiple of the continuous compactly supported function g_c (step 2), hence integrable (step 1; Integrable.const_mul). (b) Let k(y) := Dg(c·y)(c·y). Dg is continuous because g is C¹ (ContDiff.continuous_fderiv), y ↦ c·y is continuous, and the value of a continuous linear map at a vector depends continuously on both (Continuous.clm_apply), so k is continuous. The function x ↦ Dg(x)(x) vanishes at every x ∉ tsupport g, because g ≡ 0 on a neighbourhood of such an x and so Dg(x) = 0 (fderiv_of_notMem_tsupport); hence its support lies in the compact set tsupport g and it has compact support (HasCompactSupport.mono'). k is that function composed with y ↦ c·y, so k has compact support (HasCompactSupport.comp_smul, c ≠ 0). By step 1, k is integrable.
5. (Apply (H) and split the integral.) By step 2, (H) applies to h = g_c and gives ∫ (n·g(c·y) + Dg_c(y)(y)) dμ(y) = 0. Rewriting the integrand pointwise with step 3 gives ∫ (n·g(c·y) + Dg(c·y)(c·y)) dμ(y) = 0. By step 4 both summands are integrable, so the integral of the sum is the sum of the integrals (integral_add), and ∫ n·g(c·y) dμ(y) = n·∫ g(c·y) dμ(y) (integral_const_mul). Therefore n·∫ g(t⁻¹y) dμ(y) + ∫ Dg(t⁻¹y)(t⁻¹y) dμ(y) = 0. ∎
key_steps: The dilate g_t(y) = g(t⁻¹y) is C¹ (composition with the linear map y ↦ t⁻¹y) with compact support (HasCompactSupport.comp_smul).
Chain rule: Dg_t(y)(y) = Dg(t⁻¹y)(t⁻¹y) for every y.
y ↦ n·g(t⁻¹y) and y ↦ Dg(t⁻¹y)(t⁻¹y) are continuous with compact support (Dg vanishes off tsupport g), hence μ-integrable.
Apply the hypothesis to g_t, rewrite the integrand, and split with integral_add and integral_const_mul.
